analysis: Examined LocalTokenizerLoader.swift (head lines 68-139) and the new LocalTokenizerByteFallbackTests.swift. The change is a correctness fix in the decode path: LocalTokenizerBridge now precomputes heldBackBytes (byteTokens(heldBackBy:), lines 126-139) by probing the 256 `<0xHH>` tokens against the upstream tokenizer. decode (lines 108-122) appends trailing byte-token runs that swift-transformers' ByteFallbackDecoder would drop, and the result is decoded as UTF-8 with U+FFFD for invalid sequences. The change adds no network, file, key or crypto surface. The only new inputs are the model-supplied tokenizer files, which were already read before this PR, and the token IDs. Text is still produced after decryption inside the provider process and re-encrypted by the existing response path, so T-008 and A-001 handling is unchanged. Nothing touches the prefix cache (T-041), the attestation chain, authorization or the hold socket. The reverse walk is bounded by the token array length. Each non-byte token may incur one extra upstream.decode call when skipSpecialTokens is true, but the walk stops at the first non-special, non-byte token. Cost is therefore linear, and at worst O(n) per decode call. Repeated decode calls from DetokenizerV2 on a bounded segment (about 256 tokens) keep this cheap. The tokenizer is operator-controlled (A-004 and T-012 are pre-existing), so a malicious tokenizer could only change output text, which that adversary can already do. The byte-fallback outcome could differ from the old behavior only on the provider's own output, and the consumer has no integrity guarantee there anyway (T-007). Tests are test-only and write to the temp directory under random UUID names, then clean up. No security regressions were identified. Remaining limit: the upstream swift-transformers/DetokenizerV2 behavior was not supplied and was inferred from the comments and tests.
